Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 95, verses 1–3:

Page 173
Surah al-Tin

It is also called Surat al-Tin without the waw. It is Meccan according to the majority. Qatada reported that it is Medinan, and likewise from Ibn Abbas according to what is in al-Bahr and Majma' al-Bayan, through the narration of al-Mu'addal.

Ibn al-Darris, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas) what agrees with the view of the majority. The presence of a pointing indication supports this in His Exalted saying: ﴿And this secure city﴾, for by it is meant Mecca, by the consensus of the exegetes as far as we know. Its verses are eight according to all of them. When, in the preceding surah, He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the most perfect of humankind, by agreement, and indeed the most perfect of God's creation without exception, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, He, Mighty and Majestic, mentions in this surah the state of humankind in general, what its affair comes to, and what He, glory be to Him, has prepared for those among them who believed in that most perfect individual and the pride of this most exalted kind, may God bless him, grant him peace, honour him, exalt him and ennoble him. So He, Mighty, said:

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ ﴿and Mount Sinai﴾ ﴿and this secure city﴾. It is an oath by blessed, noble tracts of land according to what many have held. As for the secure city, it is Mecca, which God has protected, without any disagreement. A hadith traced to the Prophet has come: "And it is the place of the House, which is a guidance for the worlds." It was the birthplace and the place of the mission of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. "Al-Amin" is on the pattern of fa'il, either in the sense of fa'il, i.e. the one who is secure, from amina al-rajul (with the mim vowelled with damma) amanatan, so he is amin; amanun also came, as karim and kiram came, and amin is not heard as an active participle. It is heard in the sense of the relative, as in His saying: ﴿a secure sanctuary﴾, meaning possessing security. Its security is that whoever enters it is protected, as the trustworthy man protects what is entrusted to him, so there is in it a comparison to the trustworthy man. Or it is in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. the one made secure, from amannahu, meaning: he did not frighten him.

Its attribution to the land is metaphorical, and the one made secure in truth is its people; that is, their harms are not feared therein. Or the statement is elliptical and transitive, i.e. the one made secure therein from harms. The insertion of the demonstrative noun is for glorification.

As for ﴿Mount Sinai﴾, it is the mountain on which God, glory be to Him, spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, and it is called Tur Sina', with a kasra on the sin and with a long vowel, and also with a fatha on the sin and a long vowel. The first reading here in place of ﴿Sinin﴾ was recited by Umar ibn al-Khattab, Abdullah, Talha and al-Hasan, and the second by Umar also, Zayd ibn Ali, and "Tur Saynin" with a fatha on the sin, which is the dialect of Bakr and Tamim. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Amr ibn Maymun and Abu Raja' also recited with it. In al-Bahr it is stated that there is no disagreement that it is a mountain in Syria, and al-Shihab criticised this, saying that it contradicts what is well known, for the mountain known today as Tur Sina is that near the Tih, between Egypt and Aqaba. As for "Sinin", it has been said to be the name of the region in which the mountain is, to which the Tur is added, and in its inflection it is treated like Birun and the like, so it is inflected with waw and ya', and it is kept on the ya', and the nun is vowelled with the inflectional vowels.

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿Sinin﴾ is a plural in the sense of trees, its singular being sinah, so it is as if it were said: the mountain of trees.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: ﴿Sinin﴾ is al-Hasan.

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted something similar from al-Dahhak, and likewise he and a group transmitted from Ikrimah with the addition: in the language of Abyssinia. He also, with Ibn Jarir, Ibn Asakir and others, transmitted from Qatada that he said: Sinin is blessed, good, with trees, and the idafa, as mentioned, is the idafa of the attribute to the qualified noun. As for ﴿the fig and the olive﴾, a group reported from Qatada that the first of them is the mountain on which Damascus lies, and the second is the mountain on which Bayt al-Maqdis lies. It is also said, according to what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Habib al-Harith ibn Muhammad, that the first is Tur Tina and the second is Tur Zayta, because they are the places where the fig and the olive grow; and the speech on this is either by omission of a mudaf or by metonymy, in that the fig and the olive have been used metonymically for their places of growth, and this became common usage. Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu Abdullah al-Farisi that the fig is the Mosque of Damascus and the olive is Bayt al-Maqdis, and perhaps their being named thus is because in them are trees of their kind. And from Ka'b al-Ahbar that they are Damascus and Iliya, the city of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it seems that its being named so is by naming the place after its occupant. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that they are

Page 174
the Mosque of the People of the Cave and the Mosque of Iliya.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that they are the Mosque of Noah, peace be upon him, which was built upon al-Judi, and Bayt al-Maqdis. From Shahr ibn Hawshab that they are Kufa and Syria, and this was criticised on the ground that Kufa is an Islamic town which Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas founded in the days of the Commander of the Faithful Umar, may God be pleased with him; perhaps he meant the land now called Kufa, for it was, as in the Qamus and elsewhere, the dwelling of Noah, peace be upon him. Some have said: Kufa was a town before, but it was ruined and then rebuilt in the days of Umar, may God be pleased with him. It has also been said: they are two mountains between Hulwan and Hamadhan and the mountains of Syria, because they are the places where those two grow. Whichever it is, the coordinated items are consistent in that what is meant by them are specific places. It has also been said: what is meant by them are the two well-known trees.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The fig and the olive" is the fruit that people eat.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted something similar from Mujahid, and in al-Bahr it is also related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Jabir ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ikrimah and al-Hasan. On this view God, Exalted, singled out these two for swearing by from among the fruits, because they are distinguished by noble properties. The fig is a good fruit with no superior, and a delicate food that is quickly digested; it has even been said that it is the healthiest of fruits as food when eaten on an empty stomach and not followed by anything. It is also a remedy of great benefit: it opens obstructions, strengthens the liver, removes the spleen, painful urination, emaciation of the kidneys, palpitations, asthma, shortness of breath, coughing, chest pains, roughness of the windpipe, and more besides. It is related from Ali al-Rida ibn Musa al-Kazim, upon his grandfather and them be peace, that it removes bad breath, lengthens hair, and is a protection against paralysis.

Abu Dharr narrated that "a tray of figs was presented to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he ate from it and said to his companions: 'Eat. If I were to say that a fruit had descended from Paradise, I would say it is this, for the fruit of Paradise has no stones. So eat it, for it cuts off haemorrhoids and benefits gout.'"

I have not found this hadith among the muhaddithun (scholars of hadith). However, Dawud al-Tabib, after listing a number of properties of the fig and its benefit for haemorrhoids, said: it is a good hadith. It is also mentioned that its benefit for gout is when it is ground together with barley flour, wheat flour or fenugreek, and that then it benefits thick swellings and joint pains. It has other, many properties both alone and compounded, and likewise its tree, as will not be hidden from one who consults the books of medicine; and what resembles its tree is not one that influences itself, but rather a generous one that acts and does not speak.

As for the olive, it is said to be a condiment, a medicine and a fruit. They said: the calcined olive has nothing like it for digestion, for fattening, and for strengthening the limbs. Its oil suffices as a virtue, the oil with which lamps in mosques and the like are commonly lit, along with its other benefits: improving complexions, purifying humours, firming the sinews, opening obstructions, expelling worms, promoting menstruation, breaking up stones, and restoring the kidneys when drunk with hot water; and like removing whiteness of the eye, and strengthening sight when applied as kohl, and more besides. Its tree belongs to the blessed tree attested in the revelation, and if you examine the properties of its parts, it will become clear to you that it is more beneficial than the scattered remedies of the staff.

It is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that he passed by an olive tree, took a twig from it, used it as a toothstick and said: "I heard the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: 'The olive toothstick is an excellent siwak from the blessed tree; it sweetens the mouth and removes phlegm.'" And I heard him, peace and blessings be upon him, say: "It is my siwak and the siwak of the prophets before me, peace be upon them."

Some have said: the interpretation of them as stated is the correct one, and it seems that what is meant by it is the figs and olives of those holy places, and the purpose of swearing by those things is to show the nobility of the blessed places and the good and blessing that appeared in them. It returns to an oath by the blessed land and by the secure city, and in it is an allusion to the excellence of the city, as the words of the author of the Kashshaf suggest, and he clarified this in al-Kashf by saying:

That is because he distinguished the two blessings of the holy land, the worldly and the religious, by mentioning the two trees or their two fruits, and the mount on which Moses, peace be upon him, was called, and the whole group took the place of the blessed land by way of metonymy. Thus the coordination shows its fit in a clear manner, since he coordinated the city with the whole three, because they are like a single unit in this respect, as if it were said: "and the land which We have blessed in religion and in the world, and the secure city, whoever enters it in both abodes," and that is a blessing before which every blessing is diminished. It also implies that the nobility of those places lies in Moses, peace be upon him, conversing with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, for a number of days, and how many revelations came in the secure city. Then he said: and taking it literally, with the meaning of the plants or the trees, causes the relation between the first two and the secure city to be lost, because the relation of Tur Sinin to the city is not the same as its relation to them, and the speech is directed to the first. End. So reflect, for it is subtle.

Whichever it is, the answer to the oath is:

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The fig and the olive" is the fruit that people eat.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted something similar from Mujahid, and in al-Bahr it is also related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Jabir ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ikrimah and al-Hasan. On this view God, Exalted, singled out these two for swearing by from among the fruits, because they are distinguished by noble properties. The fig is a good fruit with no superior, and a delicate food that is quickly digested; it has even been said that it is the healthiest of fruits as food when eaten on an empty stomach and not followed by anything. It is also a remedy of great benefit: it opens obstructions, strengthens the liver, removes the spleen, painful urination, emaciation of the kidneys, palpitations, asthma, shortness of breath, coughing, chest pains, roughness of the windpipe, and more besides. It is related from Ali al-Rida ibn Musa al-Kazim, upon his grandfather and them be peace, that it removes bad breath, lengthens hair, and is a protection against paralysis.

Abu Dharr narrated that "a tray of figs was presented to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he ate from it and said to his companions: 'Eat. If I were to say that a fruit had descended from Paradise, I would say it is this, for the fruit of Paradise has no stones. So eat it, for it cuts off haemorrhoids and benefits gout.'"

I have not found this hadith among the muhaddithun (scholars of hadith). However, Dawud al-Tabib, after listing a number of properties of the fig and its benefit for haemorrhoids, said: it is a good hadith. It is also mentioned that its benefit for gout is when it is ground together with barley flour, wheat flour or fenugreek, and that then it benefits thick swellings and joint pains. It has other, many properties both alone and compounded, and likewise its tree, as will not be hidden from one who consults the books of medicine; and what resembles its tree is not one that influences itself, but rather a generous one that acts and does not speak.

As for the olive, it is said to be a condiment, a medicine and a fruit. They said: the calcined olive has nothing like it for digestion, for fattening, and for strengthening the limbs. Its oil suffices as a virtue, the oil with which lamps in mosques and the like are commonly lit, along with its other benefits: improving complexions, purifying humours, firming the sinews, opening obstructions, expelling worms, promoting menstruation, breaking up stones, and restoring the kidneys when drunk with hot water; and like removing whiteness of the eye, and strengthening sight when applied as kohl, and more besides. Its tree belongs to the blessed tree attested in the revelation, and if you examine the properties of its parts, it will become clear to you that it is more beneficial than the scattered remedies of the staff.

It is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that he passed by an olive tree, took a twig from it, used it as a toothstick and said: "I heard the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: 'The olive toothstick is an excellent siwak from the blessed tree; it sweetens the mouth and removes phlegm.'" And I heard him, peace and blessings be upon him, say: "It is my siwak and the siwak of the prophets before me, peace be upon them."

Some have said: the interpretation of them as stated is the correct one, and it seems that what is meant by it is the figs and olives of those holy places, and the purpose of swearing by those things is to show the nobility of the blessed places and the good and blessing that appeared in them. It returns to an oath by the blessed land and by the secure city, and in it is an allusion to the excellence of the city, as the words of the author of the Kashshaf suggest, and he clarified this in al-Kashf by saying:

That is because he distinguished the two blessings of the holy land, the worldly and the religious, by mentioning the two trees or their two fruits, and the mount on which Moses, peace be upon him, was called, and the whole group took the place of the blessed land by way of metonymy. Thus the coordination shows its fit in a clear manner, since he coordinated the city with the whole three, because they are like a single unit in this respect, as if it were said: "and the land which We have blessed in religion and in the world, and the secure city, whoever enters it in both abodes," and that is a blessing before which every blessing is diminished. It also implies that the nobility of those places lies in Moses, peace be upon him, conversing with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, for a number of days, and how many revelations came in the secure city. Then he said: and taking it literally, with the meaning of the plants or the trees, causes the relation between the first two and the secure city to be lost, because the relation of Tur Sinin to the city is not the same as its relation to them, and the speech is directed to the first. End. So reflect, for it is subtle.

Whichever it is, the answer to the oath is:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 95, verse 4:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We created man﴾ etc. By "man" (al-insan) the genus is intended, so it includes both the believer and the disbeliever, and is not specific to the latter. This is supported by the validity of the exception (istithna'), since the original state of the exception is continuity (al-ittisal).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in the best of stature﴾ is in a position of *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) relative to "man"; that is, he is existing in the best of statures. *Taqwim* means shaping, proportioning and balancing, and it is an act of God, glorious and majestic. The meaning of man's being in that state, as has been said, is that he is intimately connected with it, similar to your saying: "So-and-so is in the pleasure of Zayd," meaning that he is pleasing to him. Al-Khafaji said: it is interpreted as meaning *qawwam* (one who maintains) or *muqawwim* (one who gives form), and there is an implied genitive construction: "[the] maintenance of the best of statures," or else *fi* is superfluous (*za'ida*) and what follows it is in the position of the absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), with its adjective standing in for the verbal noun. The sense is: "We shaped him with the best of shapings." The intended meaning is that He made him in the best possible form and meaning, which includes his upright stature, the beauty of his form, his faculties of perception, the excellence of his intellect, and other things.

Whoever looks deeply into his affair and reflects on the subtleties of his outward and inward nature will see him, as one of the eminent scholars said, as "the meeting-place of the unseen and the witnessed, and the rising-place of the two luminaries of the sphere of benefiting and being benefited, the comprehensive copy of what is in the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity and all the other texts, and the commentator upon the tablet of the divine wonders deposited in him, of all that has been and all that will be." He found the truth of what has been said, and it is attributed to 'Ali, may God ennoble his face:

*Your cure is within you, though you do not perceive it; and your disease is from you, though you do not see it.*

*You think that you are a small body, while within you the greatest world is folded.*

Among what indicates the excellence of His shaping of him is that God, exalted, imprinted in him attributes that remind him of His attributes and guide him to them, so He made him knowing, willing, powerful, and so on.

And He, exalted, said: "Take on the character of God, lest it be supposed that what belongs to the master over the servant is forbidden."

In this matter, which is the decisive word, it is sufficient that God created him with His two hands, and commanded His angels, peace be upon them, to prostrate to him, while they are the honoured ones in His presence.

It has come that God created Adam in His image, and in another narration: "in the image of the Merciful."

This rules out the possibility that the pronoun refers to Adam in the sense that He created him without passing through the stages, unlike his descendants, and because he is the comprehensive copy. Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said: "Whoever knows himself, knows his Lord." People claim this is a hadith, but it is not established, as al-Nawawi said. From Yahya ibn Aktham and some of the Hanafis: they issued a legal ruling concerning a man who said to his wife: "If you are not more beautiful than the moon, then you are divorced," that the divorce does not take effect, and they cited this verse as evidence in a well-known account. Poets have, in preferring their beloved over the moon on its full night, things that the scope of enumeration cannot contain. The truth is that the difference is as clear as the dawn.

Then, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾, the "thumma" (then) indicates a temporal sequence or a sequence of rank. The "radd" (returning/rendering) may be in the sense of "ja'l" (making), in which case it takes two objects, whose original form is the subject and predicate, as in the verse:

"He turned their black hair white, and turned their white faces black."

Here "asfala" is the second object, and the meaning is: "Then We made him of the people of the Fire, who are more repugnant than every repugnant thing, and lower than every lowly thing in form and composition, because he did not conform to what We created him upon of attributes."

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "radd" is the change of state, in which case it is transitive to one object, and "asfala" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object, i.e.: "We returned him while he was more repugnant than any ugliness of face, and more hideous in creation, and they are the companions of the Fire." And it is permissible that "radd" has its well-known meaning, with "asfala" governed by the removal of the preposition, and "asfal" being treated as an adjective of a place. The intended "safilin" are the low places, i.e.: "We returned him to a place lower than the low places, which is Jahannam, or the lowest level of the Fire." The plural of "safilin" as a plural of rational beings presents a difficulty with this reading, and that it is for the rhyme (fasila) or that the verse treats them as rational beings is not something to be dwelt upon. Perhaps the preferable reading according to this is that it means "to the lowest of those who have sunk among the people of the levels (of Hell)."

ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Nakhaʿī and Qatada in one narration said: the intended meaning is his being returned to decrepitude and the weakness of the outward and inward faculties; i.e.: "Then We returned him, after that fashioning and beautifying, lower than the lowest in beauty of form and shape, when We reversed him in his creation: his back was bent after being upright, his hair turned white after being black, his skin wrinkled after being smooth, his hearing and sight dulled after being sharp, and everything about him changed: his walk became shuffling, his voice faint, his strength weakness, and his dignity senility." On this view the verse is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age﴾ and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾. This applies to the species, so it does not follow that every human is like this.

As for the grammatical analysis of "asfala," it has been said: the preceding possibilities are valid, and the most preferable of them is not hidden. Then, the context most directly suggests a reference to the state of the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection, that he will be in the most repugnant and hideous form after having been in the finest and most wondrous form, because he did not thank that blessing nor act in accordance with it. The intention of what was mentioned does not suit this; hence it has been said that it is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the apparent meaning is what fits this, as is related from al-Ḥasan, Mujahid, Abu al-ʿĀliya, Ibn Zayd and also Qatada.

And ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) read: "al-safilin" with the definite article "al-" attached.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 95, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. According to what has preceded, it is an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil) from the pronoun in "radadnahu" (We returned him), which refers back to man (al-insan); for it carries the meaning of the plural. So the believers are not returned to the lowest of the low on the Day of Resurrection, nor are their forms made ugly; rather, their radiance increases beyond their radiance and their beauty beyond their beauty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then for them is a reward never to be cut off﴾. That is: uncut (ghayr maqtu'), or not bestowed upon them with reproach (ghayr mamnun bihi 'alayhim). It confirms what the exception implies regarding their exit from the ruling of return, and it explains the manner of their condition. According to the latter view, the exception is disconnected (munqati'), the relative clause (al-mawsul) is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "for them is a reward" is its predicate (khabar). The fa' (then) is there because the subject includes the meaning of a condition (shart), and the statement carries the sense of a corrective contrast (istidrak), as if it were said: "But those who believe, for them is a reward..." etc. This is to repel the supposition that equality in the lowest age requires equality in other respects, so it is not objected that how can it be disconnected when the believers are included among those returned to the lowest age, not differing from others in the ruling.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said: the disconnection is because the exit of the believers from the ruling was not intended, and the determining factor of connection and disconnection is this (as stated in the principles of jurisprudence, usul), not exit and entry, so do not overlook this.

Many commentators took these believers to mean the righteous among the aged, as if it were said: "But those who were righteous among the aged, for them is an everlasting reward, never cut off, or not bestowed upon them with reproach, because of their patience over what they were tested with of decrepitude and old age, which prevented them from rising to perform their duties of worship."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari and Ibn Hibban narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a servant falls ill or travels, Allah, exalted is He, records for him a reward equal to what he used to do while healthy and resident."

In another narration from him: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Then for them is a reward never to be cut off﴾.

al-Tabarani narrated from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: When I test a believing servant of Mine and he praises Me for what I have tested him with, he rises from his bed like the day his mother bore him, free of sins. And the Lord, mighty and majestic, says: I have restrained this servant of Mine and tested him, so record for him what you used to record for him before that." And it is sound (sahih).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the verse: When the servant grows old and becomes weak in deeds, there is recorded for him the reward of what he used to do in his youth.

Some people took them to be the reciters of the Qur'an, and made the exception connected, excluding them from the ruling of return to the lowest age, based on what al-Hakim narrated and authenticated, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas), who said: Whoever recites the Qur'an is not returned to the lowest age; and that is His saying: ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ ﴿Except those who believe﴾, he said: except those who recited the Qur'an.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah something similar, and in it that he is not brought down to that station, meaning senility, so that anyone among the reciters of the Qur'an should not "know after knowledge anything." It is not hidden that restricting "those who believe" to what it has been restricted to is contrary to the apparent meaning. And regarding whether any of the reciters is not returned to the lowest age, there is hesitation, so let it be investigated.

The address in His words, ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgement after this?﴾, is, according to the majority of scholars (al-Jumhur), directed to mankind, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), to intensify the reproach and rebuke. The *fa'* (so) derives the rebuke from the preceding proof, and the *ba'* (by) is causal. The Judgement (*al-din*) means the recompense after resurrection. The sense is: what makes you a liar, by reason of the recompense and denying it, after this proof? The meaning is that the creation of man from a drop of semen, and his being fashioned in a form that dazzles minds and exceeds the scope of expression, or this together with his transformation from one state to another, is among the clearest proofs of the power of God, Mighty and Majestic, over resurrection and recompense. So what compels you, O man, after this decisive proof, to be a liar by denying it? For every one who denies the truth is a liar.

Qatadah, al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). That is: what makes you deny the recompense after its proof has become manifest? This is in the manner of spurring on (*al-ilhab*) and an allusion to the deniers: that is, nothing denies you the recompense after this clarification, unlike those who pay no heed to the signs of God, Exalted, and do not lift their heads to them. The interrogative is therefore for the negation of denial, and it conveys that the Messenger (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, continues in the state he is in, of not denying, because the proofs are continuous and mutually reinforcing. There is in this a subtlety not found in the first reading. On this reading it is also permissible for the *ba'* to mean *fi* (in), and for it to be causal, with an elided noun on both. The meaning would then be: what is attributed to falsehood in your report of the recompense, or by reason of your reporting it after this proof? It is also permissible for the *ba'* to be connected to the verb *yukadhdhibuka* with *al-din* taken in its meaning, so that the meaning is: what makes you a denier of the religion of Islam? This is narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah, and the interrogative is as you have heard.

It is also permissible on the first reading for *al-din* to be taken in its meaning. Some of those who held that the address is to the master of those addressed (ﷺ) made *ma* mean *man* (who), because the meaning is clearer on that basis. But this is weak, since it contradicts the familiar usage of *ma*, and so it should not be adopted when its retention in its familiar sense is sound.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 95, verse 8:

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ That is: Is not He who did what has been mentioned the most just of judges in His making and arrangement, such that one might imagine there is no resurrection and no recompense? Since it is impossible that He, glorified is He, is not the most just of judges, it is established that there is resurrection and recompense. This sentence is a confirmation of what precedes it. It has also been said: al-hukm here means al-qada' (judgment, decree), and so it is a warning to the disbelievers that He, mighty and majestic, will judge against them with the punishment they deserve. In either case, the interrogative, according to what has been said, is a confirmation of what follows a negation. What indicates this is what al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you recites 'By the fig and the olive' and reaches His saying, ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾, let him say: 'Yes, and I am among the witnesses to that.'"

It has come in some narrations that "he (ﷺ) used to say, when he reached this verse: Glory be to You, and yes (fa-bala)."

What relates to this has already been mentioned in the tafsir of the surah ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾, so refer back to it.
